sections.title: Decision and scope
paragraphs: Working location: Kajaani, Finland. Compare Québec, Canada and Singapore. Approve a capped evidence-gathering and leased-compute pilot; do not approve a 25 MW construction commitment. The Investment model ranks build, lease and a conditional 10 MW-facility hybrid using the same assumed demand. The lowest computed cost is a scenario result, not a predetermined recommendation.

Non-goals: construction-ready engineering, professional certification, real-time power control, guaranteed vendor availability or an investment guarantee. The required ten-year planning model is included; it is not an audited investment valuation. Verified university demand, signed utility offers and vendor quotes remain NULL. Numerical allowances below are separately labeled planning assumptions.

The full comparison baseline remains 20 MW IT and PUE 1.25; the hybrid builds 40% of that IT capacity only after a separate gate. Model demand is 25% of full-fleet available hours with 97% scheduling availability. Demand assumptions are independent of facility nameplate capacity; signed institutional commitments must replace them.

sections.title: Users and workload requirements
paragraphs: Illustrative workload mix: 60% research training, 25% scheduled teaching and 15% inference. These are proposed allocations, not surveyed facts. At default financial inputs the annual demand is about 30.3 million productive H100-equivalent GPU-hours. Each team must benchmark representative jobs; H100-equivalent hours cannot be assumed interchangeable with newer GPUs or LUMI's accelerator architecture.

Training: proposed jobs span 8–1,024 GPUs with checkpointing every 30 minutes; recovery target 4 hours. Teaching: reserve timetabled 1–8 GPU sessions, including 20% of teaching allocation for small institutions. Inference: essential endpoint availability target 99.9%, recovery within 1 hour, data-loss target 15 minutes through replicated checkpoints and application data. These are planning service targets; 97% scheduling availability accounts for broader batch maintenance and usable fleet time, not a claim that the essential service meets its SLA.

Security proposal: institutional federation and MFA, project isolation, least-privilege access, encryption in transit/at rest, audit logs and separate sensitive-data enclaves. Obtain each institution's data classification and residency approval before moving workloads; clinical or restricted data must not enter the shared environment until approved. This is a requirements proposal, not a certification.

Demand gate: secure funded annual commitments by workload, peak concurrency, GPU-memory needs, storage and duration. Run an 8–12 week leased/academic-access pilot; measure useful GPU-hours, job success, queue delay and cost. Procure no fleet purely from expressions of interest. At 25% full-fleet demand, 25 MW nameplate is not justified by demonstrated load.

sections.title: Three-country comparison and existing alternatives
paragraphs: Finland/Kajaani: LUMI demonstrates a local research-computing ecosystem [S1]. National 2024 electricity production is 95% fossil-free and 57% renewable [S4], which are overlapping production categories, not the site's hourly supply. FMI documents seasonal weather; freeze protection and extreme-summer cooling are both necessary [S18]. Assess CSC/LUMI allocation first [S17]; eligible academic access may avoid new infrastructure, but allocation, migration cost and workload fit are unknown.

Canada/Québec: Hydro-Québec reports annual renewable electricity above 99% [S21], with different scope from Finland's national production statistics. Projects of at least 5 MW require connection authorization [S20]. Provincial power data and low-carbon reputation do not establish spare capacity or a fixed tariff. A specific location is still needed to select ECCC station normals and extreme-weather data [S23]. Cross-Atlantic latency, data residency and support arrangements need workload testing.

Singapore: EMA's curated 2024 figures show a gas-dominated electricity mix [S5]. The meteorological service describes year-round warmth and humidity [S19], so the Kajaani cooling design cannot be transplanted unchanged. IMDA's 300 MW roadmap is an expansion ambition, not capacity allocated to this proposal [S22]. Regional research access and network connectivity may be valuable for Asian collaborators, but permitting, site water supply and electricity procurement remain unquoted.

Comparable national datacenter counts, installed capacity and site water rates remain NULL in D1. Sources differ in scope and age; no fabricated country score or universal ranking is presented. Country choice is conditional on the utility offer, workload latency, evidence of available alternatives, verified water/cooling design and like-for-like bids.

sections.title: Power and failure analysis
paragraphs: Reference 25 MW topology: two physically independent utility paths, each provisionally rated for 25 MW; sectionalized A/B switchboards; dual downstream paths to protected loads. Loss of one 25 MW transformer/path transfers protected load to the other 25 MW path. This capacity arithmetic is a design requirement, not proof that routes are independent or transfer will succeed. Loss of a shared substation is treated as total grid loss. If a downstream fault cannot be isolated, checkpoint and shed its affected training zone; essential inference is served from an independent zone or leased recovery capacity.

Standby proposal: six 5 MW usable diesel modules, with site-derated rating to be verified. Loss of one leaves 25 MW (N+1). A 10-minute UPS bridge at 25 MW requires 4.17 MWh delivered; assume 90% conversion efficiency and 80% end-of-life capacity, giving at least 5.79 MWh nameplate before further reserve. UPS protection covers necessary cooling pumps, controls and network equipment as well as IT. Start and transfer must complete within the bridge, established by integrated tests.

48-hour full-load outage: 25 × 48 = 1,200 MWh electrical output. At an unverified generator allowance of 0.25 litres/kWh and 15% unusable/reserve margin, plan 345,000 litres stored fuel. Actual manufacturer burn curves, fuel permits, tank segregation, emissions/noise and winter starting must be checked. Fuel includes a reserve and assumes no resupply. If a second generator fails, shed at least 5 MW of facility load; throttle training first, protect checkpoint/storage/control and essential inference. The proposal does not claim 48-hour availability until tests establish cooling, switching, fuel and failure independence.

No solar/wind/gas capacity is credited. UPS batteries bridge minutes, not two days. Any future renewable/storage addition needs hourly weather, demand, equipment availability and state-of-charge simulations with worst-case multi-day events; annual energy matching cannot establish uptime.

sections.title: Cooling networking storage and environmental effects
paragraphs: Use direct-to-chip liquid cooling for compatible high-density servers, plus residual air cooling, CDUs, closed loops, dry coolers and supplemental refrigeration. Provisionally specify six 5 MW heat-rejection trains, five sufficient after one fails; verify thermal capacity at extreme ambient conditions, parasitic power, shared headers and pump failure. The 25 MW thermal envelope is conservative and must be reconciled with actual heat paths. The DGX H100 power reference [S15] is not a claim that that air-cooled product is the selected liquid-cooled server.

Propose two externally diverse 100 Gbit/s links; either supports essential traffic only unless measurements prove otherwise. Internal GPU fabric must support the largest distributed job without oversubscription that invalidates cloud comparisons. Initial storage allowance is 5 PB usable parallel storage with 50 GB/s aggregate throughput, plus independent immutable backup; both are planning assumptions included in installed-IT cost, pending workload measurement and quotes.

Annual and peak water use remain NULL: a closed loop still needs filling, makeup, sanitation and fire water. Obtain a municipal service letter and cooling-vendor water balance. Do not claim zero water or guaranteed heat-sale revenue. Assess land use, construction traffic, emergency diesel noise/emissions and heat rejection with the permitting authorities before selecting a site.

Grid impact: disclose full coincident peak, ramp rates, harmonics and interruptible training capacity to the utility. Price dedicated network upgrades explicitly rather than assume existing customers pay. Compare peak curtailment and staged connection. Hourly consumption/emissions and embodied GPU/building impacts need further data; national production mix alone cannot establish project carbon benefits.

sections.title: Financing and risk allocation
paragraphs: Development equity gate: member-approved capped diligence budget, workload pilot, site options, initial utility feasibility, independently checked cost model and named project owner. Only small reversible commitments before these are resolved. Construction debt gate: signed funded member reservations, binding grid terms and schedule, land/permits, fixed or bounded EPC price, contingency, insurance and independent engineering review. Equipment finance gate: energization and cooling commissioning milestones, acceptance benchmarks and staged GPU delivery.

Illustrative finance in the model draws 50% of initial capital cost as debt and amortizes principal over eight operating years at 4% real interest. These are assumptions, not bank terms. Replacement capex is member-funded. Outstanding year-10 debt is disclosed. Resource NPV excludes financing cash flows to avoid counting capital twice; member funding includes debt draw, interest and repayments.

If power is late: consortium equity funds uncovered holding and bridge-compute costs; negotiate utility milestones and EPC delay remedies, but credit no compensation until contracted. Tie GPU delivery to energization. If demand falls: members bear committed fixed-cost reservations, reduce uncommitted expansion and resell/redeploy equipment subject to conservative recovery assumptions. If a major member exits: require a termination payment covering its noncancelable commitments; remaining institutions vote on downsizing before accepting extra exposure.

sections.title: Ownership governance and approval gates
paragraphs: If construction is approved, a consortium nonprofit owns land/facility/common infrastructure and the selected GPU fleet. Contract specialist construction, operations, utility supply, hardware support and network service. Member-supplied GPUs require interface, security and cost-allocation agreements; do not count them as free capacity.

One institution one board vote, with an independent technical/security committee and published conflict-of-interest rules. Annual allocations: 60% research, 25% teaching, 15% inference initially; review actual demand quarterly. Reserve small-institution teaching access. Cap any one institution's routine reserved capacity at 30% unless an open board vote funds additional capacity without consuming others' allocations. These are governance proposals.

Price using a transparent fixed reservation fee for committed capacity plus metered variable charges; publish utilization, idle reservations, queue times and subsidies. Release unused reservations to a preemptible common pool. New members fund incremental capacity and accept the same security rules. Resolve scheduling disputes first through the operations committee, then board appeal; emergencies prioritize safety and essential service.

Three findings most likely to reverse the recommendation: (1) binding demand and access tests show sustained useful demand beyond existing academic/commercial supply; (2) a site utility offer and integrated failure study establish affordable reliable power; (3) comparable delivered-compute quotations and benchmarked utilization change the ten-year cost ranking. Run the financial controls before choosing a phase size. No 25 MW construction approval is supported by the current uncontracted evidence.
